question: does a fresh conversion of the published hydrated recipe reproduce the published checkpoint byte for byte?

published_run.pinned_digests: receipts/hydrated-SHA256SUMS (16 files); the tree on this box was re-verified against it before the comparison ran

converter.worktree_diff_note: the published build recorded the commit but not a digest of the working-tree patch it ran with, so the local allocation patch's exact state at that moment is unrecorded. The rebuild's is recorded below, and it equals the digest the error-driven build recorded on 2026-08-16, so the converter source has not moved since at least then.

converter_repeat_control.what: two runs of the identical conversion, same box, same flags, same source, minutes apart, compared on the converter's own printed per-module quantization error and global scale
converter_repeat_control.why_it_exists: the first attempt died at compile_model on the missing marisa_trie with every module already quantized; the retry started a new job and re-quantized all of them, so one log holds the same conversion twice
converter_repeat_control.resolution_note: the converter prints proxy_err to six decimals, so this detects a difference only when it reaches that digit; it is a LOWER bound on how many modules actually differ, never an upper one. Two identical float computations round identically, so every disagreement here is a real difference in the underlying value.
converter_repeat_control.reading: the allocator is deterministic (every module got the same width) and the global scale search is deterministic (no disagreements), but the quantization result is not: 6 of 212 modules land on a different error. A conversion of this model with this converter on this card is therefore not reproducible bit for bit even against itself, which is sufficient on its own to explain a checkpoint that does not match a published one.

answer.plain: No. A fresh conversion of the published hydrated recipe does NOT reproduce the published checkpoint byte for byte. 13 of the 16 pinned payload files are identical -- every configuration, the tokenizer, the safetensors index, quantization_config.json and quantization_manifest.json -- and the three safetensors shards are not.
answer.where_it_lands: the difference reaches TENSOR BYTES, not metadata. All three shards have byte-identical headers: same 2,426 physical tensors, same names, dtypes, shapes and data offsets, and the same three-shard packing to the byte (8,351,643,585 / 8,442,742,474 / 4,792,879,451). Of those 2,426 tensors, 399 differ, and every single one of them is a `.trellis` payload: 399 of the 409 EXL3 trellis tensors, 97.6 %. Not one scale, norm, embedding, vision or BF16 companion tensor moved. Inside a differing trellis tensor 41-92 % of the bytes differ (mean 82 %), which is what a different trellis solution looks like, not a bit flip.
answer.recipe_reproduces_exactly: everything a recipe is supposed to fix came out identical: all ten per-role byte totals (full_attention 1.260 GB, linear_attention 4.207, mlp_gate 3.568, mlp_up 3.568, mlp_down 4.281, lm_head 0.954, embed 2.543, vision 0.921, mtp 0.283, norms 0.001), 21,586,964,548 B of payload, 1,199 logical tensors, 715 tensor_storage entries, and every module's assigned width.
answer.why: the converter is not deterministic, and that is measured here rather than inferred: see converter_repeat_control. Two runs of the IDENTICAL conversion in this same session -- same box, same flags, same source, minutes apart -- agreed on every module's width and every global scale but disagreed on the converter's own printed proxy error for 6 of the 212 modules the comparison could reach, at the sixth decimal the log prints. Two identical float computations round identically, so those are real differences in the quantization result. A rebuild that does not match a published checkpoint therefore needs no toolchain explanation at all.
answer.second_and_separate_finding: the published build's environment cannot be reconstructed from our records. This recipe reaches `import marisa_trie` twice -- at compile_model and again in util/add_quant_config.py -- and neither call is conditional. The pinned image receipts/release-evidence-hydrated.json names for the published build has no marisa_trie, so that image alone provably cannot run this conversion to completion. Something in the published run's environment supplied it and nothing recorded what. This does not explain the tensor difference (the repeat control already does), but it does mean the published build is not re-enterable, only re-attemptable.
what_it_means_for_reconstruction_claims: The published bytes are the artifact. The recipe is not: it fixes the composition, the widths and the byte budget exactly, and it does not fix the weights. Anyone who rebuilds from docs and receipts gets a sibling of the published checkpoint, not the published checkpoint, and must not claim otherwise.

Every fidelity number we publish is a measurement OF THE PUBLISHED BYTES, which are what the SHA256SUMS in each repo pin and what a downloader receives. Those claims are unaffected. What is affected is any claim of the form 'rebuild this and you will get our numbers': a rebuild reproduces the recipe and should land within measurement resolution, but that is now an expectation to be tested, not an identity. It has not been tested here -- the sibling was never scored, because scoring it answers a different question than the one asked.

It also puts a floor under any future byte-level comparison in this project: two conversions differ, so a diff between a rebuild and a published tree can never be read as evidence of tampering, corruption or a changed recipe until it is first shown to exceed this floor.

It does not touch the runtime's weight-RECONSTRUCTION path (reconstruct_fp8_slice, the reconstructed-prefill kernels). That is a claim about turning stored trellis bytes back into weights deterministically at load, and nothing here bears on it. The two senses of 'reconstruction' should not be conflated.
answer.what_would_settle_the_mechanism: not attempted here: identify the nondeterministic reduction. The candidates are the Hessian accumulation and the LDLQ/trellis search, both of which run in CUDA kernels whose reduction order is not pinned. A cheap next test is one module quantized twice in one process from one captured Hessian: if it still differs, the nondeterminism is in the quantizer rather than in capture.

released.recompute_cost: about 40 minutes of GPU on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell for a plain hydrated conversion plus its compile and finalize chain. This run cost about 2 hours because the first attempt died at compile_model on the missing marisa_trie and the second was killed by a harness deadline; neither wrote resume state, because the published recipe passes no -cpi and exllamav3 only resumes on an explicit --resume.
released.not_preserved_because: a second sibling of a published checkpoint is worth less than the 40 minutes of disk pressure it costs, and its interesting content -- that it differs, where, and by how much -- is entirely in this receipt. Re-running it produces a THIRD distinct checkpoint, which is the finding.
